consensus_summary: Primary consensus identifies the great fish as the typological sign of Christ’s death, burial, and resurrection (three days in the tomb/Sheol), simultaneously an instrument of divine judgment and providential deliverance for Jonah; chaos-monster, imperial-exile, baptismal, and non-symbolic readings are secondary or minority.
book_summary: The great fish/sea-monster is a great ruler among the peoples who personally heads and stands for his kingdom/state/administration (Pharaoh for Egypt, Nebuchadnezzar for Babylon, Caesar for Rome), swallowing through the body he heads and later forced to disgorge what was swallowed.
consensus_core_identification: Jonah’s great fish as Christological type of the tomb/Sheol plus appointed providential agent
book_core_identification: personal head of an empire/kingdom (Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, Caesar) who swallows and must disgorge
boundary_disagreement: Consensus primary (and most alternatives) centers on the Jonah narrative’s fish as death-realm or chaos power; book re-centers the term on human imperial rulers via dragon/whale metaphors, treating the Jonah typology only as a noted common view outside its own entry.
material_contradiction: The book’s referent (a ruling person who embodies his state) cannot be the same as the consensus primary referent (the fish that swallowed Jonah as type of Christ’s tomb); accepting one as the identification displaces the other.
rationale: Blind responses converge on the Sign-of-Jonah / Sheol / providence reading as settled primary meaning, listing the hostile-empire or Pharaoh-as-dragon sense only as a minority alternative. The book entry makes that minority sense its sole definitional core, explicitly illustrated by Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar and Caesar; the two cores are therefore incompatible identifications of the same term, yielding DIVERGENT rather than REFINED or NOVEL.
strongest_objection: Because the imperial-swallowing reading appears among the listed alternatives and the book itself flags the Christological view as ‘commonly taught,’ one could argue the book merely elevates a recognized minority strand rather than truly contradicting consensus.
